# Oral cavity

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Ear, nose, and throat > Basics of ENT > Oral cavity*

[Original Article Link](/library/jp0_6S)

---

## Summary

The mouth is the facial opening of the <u>gastrointestinal tract</u>. The oral cavity, which is bounded by the <u>lips</u> anteriorly, cheeks laterally, and the <u>oropharynx</u> posteriorly, encloses the <u>tongue</u>, palates, <u>gums</u>, and <u>teeth</u>. The mouth's primary function is the initiation of the digestion process, which involves ingestion, chewing to break down food (<u>mastication</u>), the release of digestive enzymes from the <u>salivary glands</u> into the oral cavity, and <u>swallowing</u> (<u>deglutition</u>). Secondary functions include <u>taste</u> (<u>gustation</u>), <u>sound production</u> and speech articulation, ventilation, facial expression, and touch. The oral cavity can be anatomically divided into the <u>oral vestibule</u>, the space between the <u>teeth</u> and the <u>mucosa</u> of the <u>lips</u> and cheeks, and the <u>oral cavity proper</u>, the space bounded anteriorly and laterally by the <u>teeth</u> and posteriorly by the <u>oropharynx</u>. The <u>teeth</u> are hard, calcified structures used for sound articulation as well as biting and masticating food. The oral cavity is separated from the nasal cavity by the <u>palate</u>, which is divided into the soft and the <u>hard palate</u>. The masticatory movements of the <u>jaw</u> are enabled by the <u>muscles of mastication</u>, and <u>swallowing</u> is facilitated by the palatine muscles. The <u>tongue</u> is the organ responsible for the gustatory sense, which occurs via stimulation of the <u>taste buds</u> situated in the <u>lingual papillae</u>. The oral cavity is, furthermore, a secondary respiratory channel, which communicates with the nasal cavity posteriorly.

---

## Anatomy

### Overview




The oral cavity is divided into two spaces: the <u>oral vestibule</u> and the <u>oral cavity proper</u>.









#### Anatomical boundaries




* Oral vestibule

* <u>Anterior</u>/<u>lateral</u>: buccal <u>mucosa</u> (i.e., <u>mucosa</u> of the cheeks and the <u>lips</u>)

* <u>Posterior</u>/<u>medial</u>: <u>anterior</u> (facial) surface of the <u>teeth</u> and the <u>gingiva</u> (<u>gums</u>) facing the buccal <u>mucosa</u>

* Oral cavity proper

* <u>Anterior</u>/<u>lateral</u>: <u>posterior</u> surface of the <u>teeth</u> and <u>gums</u>

* Superior (roof): soft and <u>hard palate</u>

* Inferior (floor): floor of the mouth

* <u>Posterior</u>: communicates with the <u>oropharynx</u>





#### Anatomical structures




| <br>Structures of the oral cavity<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
| <u>Lips</u> | <br><br>* Form the <u>oral fissure</u>, which is the opening of the oral cavity<br><br>* Can be divided anatomically and histologically into three regions: external facial <u>skin</u>, <u>vermillion zone</u>, and internal <u>mucosa</u>.<br><br><br> |
| Oral (buccal) <u>mucosa</u> | <br><br>* <u>Mucous membrane</u> lining the sides of the <u>oral vestibule</u> and the floor of the mouth to the <u>gums</u><br><br>* <u>Nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium</u> with no <u>sebaceous glands</u> or <u>hair follicles</u><br><br>* Composed of the following:<br><br>* Lining <u>mucosa</u>, which covers the <u>lips</u>, the cheeks, the floor of mouth, and the <u>ventral</u> surface of the <u>tongue</u><br><br>* Masticatory <u>mucosa</u>, which covers the <u>palate</u> and <u>gums</u><br><br>* Specialized <u>mucosa</u>, which covers the <u>dorsal</u> surface and <u>lateral</u> borders of the <u>tongue</u> (carry nerve endings for sensory and <u>taste</u> perception)<br><br><br> |
| Intermaxillary commissure | <br>* The space behind the last <u>molars</u> that allows communication between the <u>oral vestibule</u> and <u>oral cavity proper</u> even when the <u>teeth</u> are in occlusion<br><br> |
| <u>Teeth</u> | <br><br>* Hard, calcified structures used to break down food<br><br>* Embedded in the alveolar processes of the <u>mandible</u> and <u>maxilla</u> (see “<u>Teeth</u>” below)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Gingiva</u> | <br><br>* <u>Mucosal</u> tissue covering the surfaces of the <u>maxilla</u> and <u>mandible</u> in the oral cavity.<br><br>* It surrounds the alveolar surfaces of the <u>maxilla</u> and <u>mandible</u> and protects the roots of the <u>teeth</u> and the underlying bone (see “<u>Gingiva</u>” below)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Salivary glands</u> | <br><br>* <u>Exocrine glands</u> that produce saliva, which reaches the oral cavity via a system of ducts<br><br>* Include three paired major glands (<u>parotid</u>, <u>submandibular gland</u>, and <u>sublingual gland</u>) and hundreds of minor <u>salivary glands</u><br><br>* The ducts from <u>parotid</u> and some minor <u>salivary glands</u> open into the <u>oral vestibule</u>.<br><br>* Ducts from <u>submandibular gland</u>, <u>sublingual gland</u>, and other minor <u>salivary glands</u> open into the <u>oral cavity proper</u>.<br><br><br> |
| <u>Tongue</u> | <br><br>* Muscle involved in <u>gustation</u>, <u>mastication</u>, <u>sound production</u>, and speech articulation<br><br>* Located on the floor of the <u>oral cavity proper</u> (see “<u>Tongue</u>” below)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Palate</u> | <br><br>* Consists of an <u>anterior</u>, bony part (<u>hard palate</u>) and a <u>posterior</u> muscular part (<u>soft palate</u>)<br><br>* Separates the oral cavity from the nasal cavity (oral cavity roof)<br><br>* Muscles of the <u>soft palate</u> are involved in ventilation and <u>deglutition</u><br><br>* Both hard and soft palates are important for <u>sound production</u> and speech articulation (see “<u>Palate</u>” below)<br><br><br> |





![Midsagittal section of the head and neck](media/spuhbbn9qjxs21lwfy5x4ijs.jpg)

Midsagittal section of the head and neck

## Lips

### Overview




The <u>lips</u> form the oral fissure, which is the opening of the mouth leading into the <u>oral vestibule</u>.




### Structure




Can be divided anatomically and histologically into three regions:




* Facial <u>skin</u> (external)

* Nasolabial folds: extend from the edge of the nose to the corners of the mouth

* Philtrum: the vertical groove between the middle of the upper lip and the nose

* <u>Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium</u>, containing <u>hair follicles</u> and <u>sebaceous glands</u>

* Vermilion zone (external and internal) 

* Zone of transition between facial <u>skin</u> and lip <u>mucosa</u>

* Can be divided into dry <u>vermillion</u> (external) and wet <u>vermillion</u> (internal)

* Vermilion border (external): the line of demarcation between the highly keratinized <u>squamous epithelium</u> of the facial <u>skin</u> and the less keratinized <u>epithelium</u> of the <u>vermillion zone</u>

* Labial commissures (external and internal): corners of the mouth

* <u>Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium</u> penetrated by short <u>dermal papillae</u> that contain fewer <u>sebaceous glands</u> than the facial <u>skin</u> and no <u>hair follicles</u>.

* <u>Mucosa</u> (internal): <u>nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium</u> of the buccal <u>mucosa</u> with no <u>sebaceous glands</u> or <u>hair follicles</u>





![Histology of the lip](media/etiho3tgpbyezdtdhzco5crm.jpg)

Histology of the lip




### <u>Embryology</u> [[1]](/library/mTYVro)[[2]](/library/5TYiro)[[3]](/library/MTYMro)




* Development of the upper lip

* The maxillary prominences grow medially and fuse with the <u>lateral</u> nasal prominence, giving rise to the <u>lateral</u> parts of the upper lip.

* The maxillary prominences continue to grow medially and fuse with the <u>medial</u> nasal prominence on either side; , bringing the nostrils closer together at approx. 5 weeks' development; disruption of this process leads to <u>cleft lip</u>.

* Fusion of the <u>medial</u> nasal prominences forms the <u>philtrum</u> and middle ⅓ of the upper lip, the <u>primary palate</u>, the central nose, and the <u>nasal septum</u>

* Development of the lower lip: Fusion of the right and left mandibular processes forms the lower lip and the <u>mandible</u>

## Tongue

### Structure




* Location: on the floor of the oral cavity

* Parts

* Body: <u>anterior</u> two-thirds

* Root: <u>posterior</u> one-third

* Apex: tip of the <u>tongue</u>

* Body and root of the tongues are divided by the V-shaped sulcus terminalis

* Left and right half are divided by the sulcus medianus

* Attachments

* <u>Hyoid bone</u>

* <u>Mandible</u>

* <u>Palate</u>

* <u>Styloid process of the temporal bone</u>

* <u>Pharynx</u>





### Function




* <u>Gustation</u>

* Speech and <u>sound production</u>

* <u>Mastication</u> and <u>deglutition</u>

* Touch





### <u>Histology</u>




The <u>tongue</u> consist of the following layers:




* <u>Mucous membrane</u>

* Dorsum has a velvety appearance due to the presence of numerous <u>papillae</u>

* Inferior surface appears smooth and thin

* <u>Epithelium</u>

* Keratinized surface

* <u>Nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium</u>

* Muscle layer (<u>skeletal muscle</u>)

* Corium: <u>connective tissue</u> with mucous and <u>serous glands</u>

* <u>Adipose tissue</u>





![Fine structure of the tongue](media/klfkms7awm730ml04wqcpzzp.jpg)

Fine structure of the tongue

![Epithelium of the dorsal tongue](media/il155oz9uasd8anqqgg2sdhg.jpg)

Epithelium of the dorsal tongue




### Lingual papillae




* <u>Lingual papillae</u> represent small <u>mucosal</u> projections that cover the <u>dorsal</u> surface of the <u>tongue</u>.

* Increase the surface area of the <u>tongue</u>

* Located on the dorsum of the <u>tongue</u>, mostly on the <u>anterior</u> two-thirds

* Some <u>papillae</u> contain <u>taste buds</u>, <u>clusters</u> of 50–150 <u>taste</u> <u>receptor</u> cells responsible for <u>gustation</u>    [[4]](/library/aOYQI6)





| <u>Lingual papillae</u> type | Characteristics | Innervation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Filiform papillae | <br><br>* Most numerous type of the <u>lingual papillae</u><br><br>* Follow the V shape of the sulcus terminalis throughout the <u>anterior</u> two-thirds of the <u>tongue</u>, becoming more transverse at the tip of the <u>tongue</u><br><br>* Slender, small, and conical in shape<br><br>* The only keratinized <u>papillae</u><br><br>* Responsible for<br><br>* Sensation of touch<br><br>* Increasing friction between the <u>tongue</u> and the food to facilitate <u>mastication</u> and digestion<br><br>* The only <u>papillae</u> without <u>taste buds</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Lingual nerve</u> of the <u>mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve</u> (<u>CN V<sub>3</sub></u>) for sensation of touch<br><br> |
| Fungiform papillae | <br><br>* Located on both sides of the body of the <u>tongue</u> and the apex<br><br>* Mushroom-shaped<br><br>* Deep red color is due to highly vascularized <u>connective tissue</u> core<br><br>* Contain very few <u>taste buds</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Chorda tympani</u> of the <u>facial nerve</u> (<u>CN VII</u>) for <u>taste</u> sensation<br><br> |
| Foliate papillae | <br><br>* Located in front of the palatoglossal arches and the <u>lingual tonsils</u>, on both sides of the <u>tongue</u><br><br>* Rudimentary in humans<br><br>* Leaf-shaped<br><br>* Contain abundant <u>taste buds</u><br><br><br> |  |
| <br>Circumvallate papillae <br> | <br><br>* The largest of the <u>papillae</u><br><br>* 8–12 in number<br><br>* Follow the V shape of the sulcus terminalis anteriorly<br><br>* Dome-shaped (narrower at the base and larger at the apex)<br><br>* Surrounded by a slight circular <u>mucosal</u> elevation (vallum or wall) which is separated from the <u>papilla</u> by a circular sulcus<br><br>* Covered by <u>stratified</u> <u>squamous epithelium</u><br><br>* Contain abundant <u>taste buds</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Glossopharyngeal nerve</u> (<u>CN IX</u>) for <u>taste</u> sensation<br><br>* The only part of the <u>anterior</u> two-thirds of the <u>tongue</u> that is not innervated by the <u>CN V<sub>3</sub></u> or <u>CN VII</u><br><br><br> |

### Lingual tonsils




* Characteristics 

* Located at the base of the <u>tongue</u> bilaterally

* Two small aggregates of lymphoid tissue

* Covered by <u>nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium</u>

* Surrounded by a thin capsule

* Function: immune protection (contain <u>T cells</u> and <u>B cells</u>, which produce <u>IgA</u>)

* Blood supply

* <u>Lingual artery</u> (branch of the <u>external carotid artery</u>)

* Facial <u>artery</u> (tonsillar branch)

* Ascending pharyngeal branch (<u>external carotid artery</u>)

* Innervation: tonsillar branches of the <u>glossopharyngeal nerve</u> (<u>CN IX</u>)

Location of tonsils

![Lingual tonsil](media/qbrcylry76rplmysqvkwaa7j.jpg)

Lingual tonsil




### Muscles of the <u>tongue</u>




#### Extrinsic muscles of the tongue




The <u>extrinsic muscles of the tongue</u> originate outside of the <u>tongue</u>.




| Muscle | Origin | Insertion | Innervation | Function |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| <u>Palatoglossus</u> | <br>* Palatine <u>aponeurosis</u> (<u>aponeurosis</u> of the <u>soft palate</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Posterolateral sides of the <u>tongue</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Vagus nerve</u> (<u>CN X</u>), via the pharyngeal plexus<br><br> | <br><br>* Elevation of the back of the <u>tongue</u><br><br>* <u>Depression</u> of the <u>soft palate</u><br><br><br> |
| Genioglossus | <br>* <u>Mandible</u> (genial tubercle)<br><br> | <br><br>* Body of the <u>hyoid bone</u><br><br>* Inferior surface of the <u>tongue</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Hypoglossal nerve</u> (<u>CN XII</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Protrusion and <u>depression</u> of the <u>tongue</u><br><br> |
| Hyoglossus | <br>* <u>Hyoid bone</u> (greater horn and body)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Lateral</u> and inferior surface of the <u>tongue</u> (<u>lateral</u> to the <u>genioglossus</u> and <u>medial</u> to the <u>styloglossus</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Retraction</u> and <u>depression</u> of the <u>tongue</u><br><br> |  |
| Styloglossus | <br>* <u>Temporal bone</u> (styloid process)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Lateral</u> and inferior surface of the <u>tongue</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Elevation of the sides of the <u>tongue</u> to facilitate <u>swallowing</u><br><br>* <u>Retraction</u> of the <u>tongue</u><br><br><br> |  |





> [!NOTE]
> The <u>genioglossus</u> normally protrudes the <u>tongue</u> evenly in the midline, but if there is unilateral hypoglossal damage, the <u>tongue</u> will deviate towards the side of the damage.




> [!NOTE]
> The Genie propels out of the bottle (the genioglossus protrudes the <u>tongue</u>).

#### Intrinsic muscles of the tongue




The <u>intrinsic muscles of the tongue</u> originate and insert within the <u>tongue</u>.




| Muscle | Origin | Insertion | Innervation | Function |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Superior longitudinal muscle | <br>* Median fibrous septum, close to the <u>epiglottis</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Lateral</u> edges of the <u>tongue</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Hypoglossal nerve</u> (<u>CN XII</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Retracts</u> the <u>tongue</u>, making it short and thick<br><br> |
| Inferior longitudinal muscle | <br>* Root of the <u>tongue</u><br><br> | <br>* Apex of the <u>tongue</u><br><br> |  |  |
| Vertical muscle | <br>* Dorsum of the <u>tongue</u> (<u>submucosal</u> <u>fibrous layer</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Anterior</u> borders of the <u>tongue</u><br><br> | <br>* Flattens and broadens the <u>tongue</u><br><br> |  |
| Transverse muscle of the tongue | <br>* Median fibrous septum<br><br> | <br>* <u>Lateral</u> edges of the <u>tongue</u><br><br> | <br>* Narrows and elongates the <u>tongue</u><br><br> |  |





### <u>Blood vessels</u> and nerve supply of the <u>tongue</u>




| Structure | Characteristics |
| --- | --- |
| Arterial supply | <br>* Lingual artery<br><br>* Branch of the <u>external carotid artery</u> (at the level of the <u>hyoid bone</u> in the <u>carotid triangle</u>)<br><br>* Branches<br><br>* Sublingual <u>artery</u><br><br>* <u>Dorsal</u> <u>lingual artery</u><br><br>* Suprahyoid <u>artery</u><br><br>* Deep <u>lingual artery</u> (terminal branch of the <u>lingual artery</u>)<br><br> |
| Venous drainage | <br><br>* Lingual veins<br><br>* Originate on the dorsum, sides, and inferior surfaces of the <u>tongue</u><br><br>* Drain into the <u>internal jugular vein</u><br><br>* Follow the course of the <u>lingual artery</u><br><br>* Ranine <u>vein</u><br><br>* Begins on the tip of the inferior <u>tongue</u><br><br>* Follows the course of the <u>hypoglossal nerve</u><br><br>* Other <u>veins</u><br><br>* Sublingual <u>vein</u><br><br>* <u>Dorsal</u> <u>lingual vein</u><br><br>* Suprahyoid <u>vein</u><br><br>* Deep <u>lingual vein</u><br><br>* These <u>veins</u> are the route of absorption for sublingual <u>nitroglycerin</u>.<br><br><br> |
| <br>Innervation  <br> | <br><br>* Motor innervation<br><br>* <u>Hypoglossal nerve</u> (<u>CN XII</u>): <u>hyoglossus</u>, <u>genioglossus</u>, and <u>styloglossus muscles</u><br><br>* <u>Vagus nerve</u> (<u>CN X</u>): <u>palatoglossus muscle</u><br><br>* Sensory innervation<br><br>* <u>Anterior</u> two-thirds of the <u>tongue</u> (excluding <u>papillae</u> vallatae)<br><br>* <u>Taste</u>: <u>chorda tympani</u> from <u>facial nerve</u> (<u>CN VII</u>)<br><br>* General sensation: <u>lingual nerve</u> from the <u>mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve</u> (<u>CN V<sub>3</sub></u>)<br><br>* <u>Posterior</u> one-third of the <u>tongue</u> (including <u>papillae</u> vallatae): <u>taste</u> and general sensation through <u>glossopharyngeal nerve</u> (<u>CN IX</u>)<br><br>* Epiglottic region of the <u>tongue</u> and <u>epiglottis</u>: <u>taste</u> and general sensation through <u>internal laryngeal nerve</u> from <u>vagus nerve</u> (<u>CN X</u>)<br><br><br> |





> [!NOTE]
> All of the <u>tongue</u> muscles (intrinsic and extrinsic) are innervated by the <u>hypoglossal nerve</u> (<u>CN XII</u>), except for the <u>palatoglossus</u> (<u>CN X</u>).

### <u>Embryology</u>




| Structure | Characteristics |
| --- | --- |
| <u>Anterior</u> two-thirds of the <u>tongue</u> | <br>* Develops from the <u>1<sup>st</sup> pharyngeal arch</u> <br><br>* A median swelling (median <u>tongue</u> bud or tuberculum impar) develops within the <u>1<sup>st</sup> pharyngeal arch</u> during the 4<sup>th</sup> week of <u>embryonic development</u>.<br><br>* <u>Lateral</u> lingual swellings develop on the right and left sides of the <u>1<sup>st</sup> pharyngeal arch</u> during the 5<sup>th</sup> week of <u>embryonic development</u>, expand, and cover the <u>medial</u> lingual swelling.<br><br>* The median sulcus represents the line of their fusion.<br><br> |
| <u>Posterior</u> one-third of the <u>tongue</u> | <br>* Develops from the 2<sup>nd</sup>, 3<sup>rd</sup>, and 4<sup>th</sup> <u>pharyngeal arches</u> <br><br>* A swelling (copula) develops in the midline of the <u>2<sup>nd</sup> pharyngeal arch</u> during the 4<sup>th</sup> week of <u>embryonic development</u>.<br><br>* A subsequent swelling (hypopharyngeal eminence) of <u>endoderm</u> of the 3<sup>rd</sup> and 4<sup>th</sup> <u>pharyngeal arches</u> expands and covers the copula during the 5<sup>th</sup> and 6<sup>th</sup> weeks of <u>embryonic development</u>.<br><br> |
| Foramen cecum (tongue) | <br><br>* Located at the intersection between the sulcus terminalis and sulcus medianus<br><br>* Site of embryonic origin of the <u>thyroglossal duct</u><br><br><br> |
| Muscles of the <u>tongue</u> | <br>* Both the intrinsic and <u>extrinsic muscles of the tongue</u> are derived from myoblasts of occipital <u>somites</u> that migrate towards the <u>tongue</u>.<br><br> |

## Palate

### Overview




* The <u>palate</u> divides the oral cavity from the nasal cavity.

* Constitutes the roof of the mouth and contributes to the floor of the nose





![Midsagittal section of the head and neck](media/spuhbbn9qjxs21lwfy5x4ijs.jpg)

Midsagittal section of the head and neck




### Anatomy of the <u>definitive palate</u>




| Structure | Characteristics |
| --- | --- |
| Hard palate | <br><br>* A bony framework covered by <u>mucosa</u><br><br>* Formed by the horizontal plate of the <u>palatine bone</u> (<u>posterior</u>) and the palatal shelves of the <u>maxilla</u> (<u>anterior</u>)<br><br>* Constitutes the <u>anterior</u>, greater part of the <u>palate</u><br><br>* Contains following foramina (see also <u>skull</u>):<br><br>* <u>Incisive foramen</u><br><br>* <u>Greater palatine foramen</u><br><br>* <u>Lesser palatine foramen</u><br><br>* Receives blood supply from the greater palatine <u>arteries</u> (branches of the descending palatine <u>artery</u>, which originates from the maxillary <u>artery</u>)<br><br>* Innervated by the greater palatine and nasopalatine nerves (branches of the <u>maxillary nerve</u>)<br><br><br> |
| Soft palate | <br><br>* A fibromuscular fold that forms the <u>posterior</u> part of the <u>palate</u><br><br>* Continuous with the palatoglossal folds and the palatopharyngeal folds<br><br>* Supplied by the following branches of the <u>external carotid artery</u>:<br><br>* Ascending palatine <u>artery</u>, which arises from the facial <u>artery</u><br><br>* Palatine branches of the <u>ascending pharyngeal artery</u><br><br>* Lesser palatine <u>arteries</u>, branches of the descending palatine <u>artery</u>, which originates from the maxillary <u>artery</u><br><br>* Innervated by the lesser palatine nerve (secretomotor, sensory, and <u>taste</u>) and the <u>vagus nerve</u> (motor)<br><br><br> |





![Neuromusculature of the hard and soft palate](media/mhr0e3fx061l94042iw61pqx.jpg)

Neuromusculature of the hard and soft palate

![Sensory innervation of the nasal cavity and the palate](media/padmrp8ev2z7ustftay63wae.jpg)

Sensory innervation of the nasal cavity and the palate




### Muscles of the palate




| Muscle | Origin | Insertion | Innervation | Function |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Tensor veli palatini | <br><br>* <u>Medial pterygoid</u> plate of the <u>sphenoid bone</u> (<u>scaphoid</u> fossa)<br><br>* Auditory tube (<u>cartilaginous</u> part)<br><br><br> | <br>* Palatine <u>aponeurosis</u> (<u>aponeurosis</u> of the <u>soft palate</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve</u> (<u>CN V<sub>3</sub></u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* Tension of the <u>soft palate</u><br><br>* Opening of the auditory tube inlet during <u>deglutition</u><br><br><br> |
| Levator veli palatini | <br><br>* <u>Temporal bone</u> (petrous region)<br><br>* Auditory tube (<u>cartilaginous</u> part)<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Vagus nerve</u> (branches of the pharyngeal plexus)<br><br> | <br>* Elevation of the <u>soft palate</u><br><br> |  |
| Musculus uvulae | <br><br>* <u>Palatine bone</u> (<u>posterior</u> nasal <u>spine</u>)<br><br>* <u>Posterior</u> border of the <u>hard palate</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Palatine <u>aponeurosis</u> (<u>aponeurosis</u> of the <u>soft palate</u>)<br><br>* <u>Mucosa</u> of the uvula<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Closure of the <u>nasopharynx</u><br><br>* Uvular movement<br><br><br> |  |
| Palatoglossus | <br>* Palatine <u>aponeurosis</u> (<u>aponeurosis</u> of the <u>soft palate</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Posterolateral side of the <u>tongue</u><br><br> | <br>* Elevation of the <u>tongue</u><br><br> |  |
| Palatopharyngeus | <br><br>* <u>Thyroid</u> <u>cartilage</u><br><br>* <u>Lateral</u> sides of the <u>pharynx</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Branches of the pharyngeal plexus from:<br><br>* <u>Vagus nerve</u><br><br>* <u>Glossopharyngeal nerve</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Closure of the <u>nasopharynx</u><br><br>* Elevation of the <u>pharynx</u><br><br><br> |  |





> [!NOTE]
> In <u>vagus nerve</u> (<u>CN X</u>) lesions, the uvula deviates away from the side of the lesion.




![Muscles of the palate and extrinsic muscles of the tongue](media/uaq63dlw36qumrhaxphmn1wd.jpg)

### <u>Embryology</u>   (development of the palate)




* 4<sup>th</sup> week of development

* Downward <u>proliferation</u> of the <u>mesoderm</u> covering the forebrain → formation of the frontonasal prominence

* Local thickening of the <u>surface ectoderm</u> on both sides of the frontonasal prominence → formation of the nasal placodes

* 5<sup>th</sup> week of development: : invagination of the nasal placodes → formation of <u>medial</u> and <u>lateral</u> nasal prominences

* 6<sup>th</sup>–7<sup>th</sup> week of development

* <u>Medial</u> growth of the maxillary prominences and subsequent fusion with <u>medial</u> nasal prominences → formation of the intermaxillary segment, composed of:

* Labial component → development of <u>philtrum</u>

* Upper <u>jaw</u> component → development of the four <u>incisor</u> <u>teeth</u>

* Palatal component → development of the triangular <u>primary palate</u> (median <u>palatine process</u>)

* Development of <u>lateral</u> <u>palatine processes</u> (palatal shelves) <u>posterior</u> to the <u>primary palate</u>;   and subsequent fusion of the two palatal shelves in the midline → formation of the <u>secondary palate</u> around 8–12 weeks of development

* 7<sup>th</sup>–8<sup>th</sup> week of development: fusion of the primary and secondary palates;  at the level of the incisive foramen → formation of the <u>permanent palate</u>





| Structure | Formation | Developmental defects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Primary palate | <br>* Formed through the fusion of the <u>medial</u> nasal prominences in the midline with <u>palatine processes</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Cleft lip</u>: failed fusion of the <u>palatine processes</u> and <u>medial</u> nasal prominences<br><br> |
| Secondary palate | <br>* Formed through the fusion of the <u>lateral</u> <u>palatine processes</u> (palatal shelves), which derive from the maxillary prominences<br><br> | <br>* <u>Cleft palate</u>: failed fusion either of the palatine shelves or of the palatine shelves with the <u>nasal septum</u> and/or <u>primary palate</u><br><br> |
| Permanent palate | <br>* Formed through the fusion of the primary and secondary palates with the <u>nasal septum</u> at the level of the <u>incisive foramen</u><br><br> | <br>* N/A<br><br> |





![Development of the face and palate](media/l4fx44fgwkk1mqg7n3egvm6f.jpg)

Development of the face and palate

## Salivary glands

In addition to the three larger paired glands (<u>parotid</u>, <u>submandibular gland</u>, and <u>sublingual glands</u>), there are several hundred small <u>salivary glands</u> in the oral cavity and throat. As secretory glands, they secrete up to 1.4 L of saliva per day. The primary functions of saliva include:




* Digestion

* Protection of the <u>mucosa</u> and <u>teeth</u>

* Immunological defense

* Transport of soluble flavors to the <u>taste buds</u>





![Major salivary glands](media/vefi7u1ln351w2msjp1mgtk3.jpg)

Major salivary glands




### Parotid gland




* Located on the surface of the <u>masseter muscle</u>, <u>dorsal</u> to the mandibular ramus and ventrocaudal to the <u>external auditory canal</u> in the retromandibular fossa.

* Subdivided by the branches of the <u>facial nerve</u> which runs through the <u>parotid gland</u>

* Its salivary duct (Stensen duct) runs forward along the <u>masseter muscle</u> and opens adjacent to the 2<sup>nd</sup> molar in the vestibule of the mouth (the space between the cheeks and the <u>teeth</u>).

* Produces mainly serous fluid and ∼ 40% of the total amount of saliva.





![Parotid salivary gland (anatomic model)](media/ud9zyxv3lwl811orh2x7kn2f.jpg)

Parotid salivary gland (anatomic model)

![Innervation of the parotid gland](media/sv7i81k9t3mimsepxk4mrexs.jpg)

Innervation of the parotid gland




### Submandibular gland




* Located  <u>medial</u> and <u>caudal</u> to the inner surface of the <u>mandible</u> above the mylohyoid and <u>digastric muscles</u>

* The salivary duct (Wharton duct) ends in the <u>sublingual caruncle</u>

* Produces seromucous fluid and the greater part (∼ 50%) of the secreted saliva





### Sublingual gland




* Located <u>medial</u> to the <u>mandible</u> above the mylohyoid muscle and below the sublingual fold

* Its main salivary duct also ends in the <u>Wharton duct</u>

* Produces mainly mucous fluid

## Mastication

### Muscles of mastication




| Muscle | Origin | Insertion | Innervation |  | Function | <u>Embryology</u> |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Masseter | <br>* Zygomatic arch (lower and <u>medial</u> surface)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Mandible</u> (ramus, angle, and the <u>lateral</u> surface of the <u>coronoid process</u>)<br><br> | <br>* <u>Mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve</u> (<u>CN V<sub>3</sub></u>)<br><br> |  | <br><br>* Deep part: <u>retraction</u> of the <u>mandible</u><br><br>* <u>Superficial</u> part: elevation of the <u>mandible</u> (most powerful muscle)<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>1<sup>st</sup> pharyngeal arch</u><br><br> |
| Temporalis | <br>* <u>Temporal fossa</u><br><br> | <br>* <u>Mandible</u> (ramus and <u>coronoid process</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Elevation and <u>retraction</u> of the <u>mandible</u><br><br> |  |  |  |
| Lateral pterygoid | <br><br>* Superior head: <u>sphenoid bone</u> (<u>infratemporal fossa</u>)<br><br>* Inferior head: <u>sphenoid bone</u> (<u>lateral</u> surface of the <u>lateral pterygoid</u> plate)<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Mandible</u> (neck and <u>temporomandibular joint</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* Bilateral contraction<br><br>* Superior head: elevation of the <u>mandible</u><br><br>* Inferior head: <u>depression</u> and <u>protraction</u> of the <u>mandible</u> (major protractor)<br><br>* Unilateral contraction: laterotrusion (sideways movement) of the <u>mandible</u> to the <u>contralateral</u> side<br><br><br> |  |  |  |
| Medial pterygoid | <br><br>* <u>Superficial</u> head<br><br>* Maxillary tuberosity<br><br>* <u>Palatine bone</u> (pyramidal process)<br><br>* Deep head<br><br>* <u>Sphenoid bone</u> (<u>medial</u> surface of the <u>lateral pterygoid</u> plate)<br><br>* <u>Palatine bone</u> (pyramidal process)<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Mandible</u> (<u>medial</u> surface, angle, and ramus)<br><br> | <br>* Elevation and <u>protraction</u> of the <u>mandible</u><br><br> |  |  |  |





![Muscles of mastication](media/xf3qabyc8y14xr6pvy9jvztx.jpg)

Muscles of mastication




### Function



* <u>Mastication</u> muscles facilitate the masticatory process via the following:

* <u>Depression</u> of the <u>mandible</u> (opening the mouth), which involves the following:

* <u>Lateral pterygoid</u>

* Certain <u>suprahyoid muscles</u> (<u>anterior</u> <u>digastric</u>, geniohyoid, and mylohyoid muscles)

* Elevation of the <u>mandible</u> (closing the mouth), which involves the following:

* <u>Masseter</u> (<u>superficial</u> part)

* <u>Temporalis</u>

* <u>Medial pterygoid</u>

* <u>Protraction</u>, which involves the following:

* <u>Lateral pterygoid</u> (major contributor)

* <u>Medial pterygoid</u>

* <u>Retraction</u>, which involves the following:

* <u>Masseter</u> (deep part)

* <u>Temporalis</u>

* Some <u>suprahyoid muscles</u> (<u>digastric</u> and geniohyoid muscles)




> [!NOTE]
> To remember the <u>muscles of mastication</u> that close the mouth: “Resist the TEMPtation to eat yuMMy food!” (TEMP = Temporalis; M = Masseter; M = Medial pterigoyd)

## Taste (gustation)

### Overview




* Definition: a chemosensory process triggered by ions and molecules in solution stimulating <u>receptors</u> located in the <u>taste buds</u>

* Location: <u>Taste buds</u> are primarily located in the <u>tongue</u>, <u>palate</u>, and <u>epiglottis</u>.

* Tastants: any molecule capable of eliciting <u>taste</u>





### Anatomy of <u>taste</u>




#### Gustatory pathway




The nerves responsible for <u>taste</u> transmit information to the <u>solitary nucleus</u> in the medulla, which in turn projects to three different <u>brain</u> areas:




* <u>Ventral posteromedial nucleus</u> (VPM) of the <u>thalamus</u>, which projects to the basal portion of the <u>postcentral gyrus</u> (conscious gustatory perception)

* <u>Hypothalamus</u> (emotional component of gustatory perception)

* <u>Amygdala</u> (emotional component of gustatory perception)





![Gustatory pathway](media/qmuch4v4vlciph6ryyh3pls8.jpg)

Gustatory pathway




#### Taste papillae and taste buds




* <u>Taste papillae</u>

* <u>Connective tissue</u> projections covered by squamous cells

* Four types

* Foliate

* Filiform

* Fungiform

* Circumvallate

* Contain different <u>types of taste</u> buds

* <u>Taste buds</u>

* Contain <u>microvilli</u> that connect to a central opening (pore)

* Tastants are sensed by <u>taste</u> <u>receptors</u> in the pore.

* Different mechanisms of <u>taste</u> signaling involve:

* Transmembrane ionic channels

* Salty (e.g., <u>sodium</u> <u>chloride</u>)

* Sour (e.g., hydrogen ions)

* <u>G protein-coupled receptors</u>

* Sweet (e.g., <u>carbohydrates</u>)

* Bitter (e.g., <u>quinine</u>, <u>nicotine</u>)

* <u>Umami</u> (e.g., <u>glutamate</u>, <u>aspartate</u>)





![Taste papillae and taste buds](media/bf9dth12jywrbj17eafblwpg.jpg)

Taste papillae and taste buds

![Primary and secondary sensory cells](media/sgo29xpm8bdi6936t661eetb.jpg)

Primary and secondary sensory cells




### Physiology of <u>taste</u>




| Types of taste | Tastant | Mechanism | Function |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Salty | <br>* Ions (e.g., Na<sup>+</sup>, NH<sup>4+</sup>, <u>K<sup>+</sup></u>, SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>, Cl<sup>−</sup>)<br><br> | <br>* Ions (e.g., <u>sodium</u> <u>chloride</u>) enter <u>the cell</u> via ionic channels → cell <u>depolarization</u> → generation of <u>action potentials</u> in nerve fibers → <u>brain</u> perception of salty <u>taste</u><br><br> | <br>* Regulation of <u>electrolyte</u> intake<br><br> |
| Sour | <br>* Hydrogen ions (H<sup>+</sup>)<br><br> | <br>* Hydrogen ions enter <u>the cell</u> via transmembrane ionic channels → acidic intracellular environment → generation of <u>action potentials</u> in nerve fibers → <u>brain</u> perception of sour <u>taste</u><br><br> | <br>* Warning signal for toxins<br><br> |
| Sweet | <br>* <u>Carbohydrates</u> and some <u>proteins</u><br><br> | <br>* Binding of <u>G protein-coupled receptors</u> (<u>gustducin</u>) → increased levels of <u>second messengers</u> (<u>inositol trisphosphate</u>, <u>IP<sub>3</sub></u>; <u>diacylglycerol</u>, <u>DAG</u>) → release of intracellular <u>calcium</u> stores into the <u>cytoplasm</u> of the cell → <u>sodium</u> influx into the cell → release of <u>ATP</u> → generation of <u>action potentials</u> in nerve fibers → <u>brain</u> perception of sweet, bitter, or <u>umami</u> <u>taste</u><br><br> | <br>* Increase appetite for calorie-dense foods<br><br> |
| Bitter | <br>* Highly variable (e.g., <u>quinine</u>, <u>nicotine</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Warning signal for toxins<br><br> |  |
| <br>Umami (savory) | <br>* Various <u>amino acids</u> (e.g., <u>glutamate</u>, <u>aspartate</u>)<br><br> | <br>* Increase appetite for protein-rich foods<br><br> |  |





![Gustatory receptor depolarization (taste sensation)](media/rbs4w4hj36z42q8sloczoyqm.jpg)

Gustatory receptor depolarization (taste sensation)

## Clinical significance

### Neurologic disorders




* <u>Facial nerve palsy</u>

* <u>Bulbar palsy</u>

* <u>Trigeminal neuralgia</u>

* <u>Trigeminal nerve lesion</u>

* <u>Glossopharyngeal nerve lesion</u>

* <u>Vagus nerve lesion</u>

* <u>Accessory nerve lesion</u> (XI)

* <u>Dysgeusia</u>

* <u>Ageusia</u>

* <u>Jugular foramen syndrome</u>

* <u>Achalasia</u>

* <u>Trismus</u>





### Inflammatory and infectious diseases




* <u>Periodontitis</u>

* <u>Pulpitis</u>

* <u>Gingivitis</u>

* <u>Acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis</u>

* <u>Acute tonsillitis</u>

* <u>Angular cheilitis</u>

* <u>Aphthous stomatitis</u>

* <u>Glossitis</u>

* <u>Hand, foot, and mouth disease</u>

* <u>Herpangina</u>

* <u>Herpes labialis</u>

* <u>Herpetic pharyngotonsillitis</u>

* <u>Ludwig angina</u>

* <u>Oral hairy leukoplakia</u>

* <u>Oropharyngeal candidiasis</u> (<u>oral thrush</u>)










### Immunologic disorders




* <u>Sjogren syndrome</u>

* <u>Angioedema</u>

* <u>Myasthenia gravis</u>





### Congenital diseases and dysmorphisms




* <u>Macroglossia</u>

* <u>Osteogenesis imperfecta</u>

* <u>Hutchinson teeth</u>

* <u>Gardner syndrome</u>

* <u>Cleft lip and cleft palate</u>





### <u>Neoplastic</u> disorders




* <u>Oral cavity cancer</u>

* Throat cancer (<u>squamous cell carcinoma</u> of the tonsil)





### <u>Dental injuries</u>




* <u>Dental avulsion</u>

* <u>Dental subluxation</u>

* <u>Dental fracture</u>





### Other disorders




* <u>Obstructive sleep apnea</u> (can be exacerbated by <u>hypertrophy</u> of the <u>lingual tonsils</u>)

* <u>Bruxism</u>
